decisions.issues: v06 is clean. Nagoji matches his sheet: thick curled moustache, clean chin with light stubble, gold ear stud, loose curly hair, ochre tunic, bandaged hands, and the tunic flap covers his left forearm. His hinged collar has an empty side ring, his wrist manacles are joined by a short chain and his ankles by a hobble chain. Keshavrao matches his lock: short ragged hair, faint moustache, grey-brown tunic, no ear stud, unbandaged hands, empty collar, wrist chain and hobble. The freed pen chain whips loose and splashes into the water between them, both men stagger apart and look up, and the setting stays inside the closed, lantern-lit hold. Lighting and water level match the chosen 5.4 (v09). There is no text, noose or gore. The panel has no lettering. Minor points that do not block the pick: both men are more muscular than the 'narrow shoulders' note suggests, and the water is shin-deep rather than the waist-deep of 4.5, but it matches the adjacent 5.4. Rejected v03 as backup: Keshavrao's hands are bandaged, which breaks his 'thin unbandaged hands' lock. Each of Nagoji's manacles also trails its own dangling chain instead of a single short chain joining the wrists, so the irons read as broken.

Neither candidate is acceptable. v08 (the regeneration) puts a gallery of armed Portuguese soldiers inside the hold at upper right: morions, steel cuirasses, red sleeves, halberds and a lantern, with another morion behind Keshavrao. That breaks the script's standing rule that no guard enters the hold, contradicts 6.2 ('If we take it, they will shoot us') and the guard's entrance down the ladder in 6.5, and the costume is wrong for the chapter's guards, who wear buff leather jerkins. The hazy beige void at its upper left also reads as fog or open air, not a closed deck ceiling. Its good points are worth keeping: Nagoji is on model (curled moustache, clean chin, gold stud, collar ring at the side), a freed chain splashes into the water at left, and two men at right strain at a ring that holds. v07 is clean and on model and matches 5.4's flooded hold. However, the FIVE-LENS-REVIEW-r2 finding (fidelity, confirmed major) holds on re-inspection: every background prisoner copies the leads' hauling pose like a galley crew, no section's chain clearly drops free, and nobody is left staring after the pair. v07 also lights the hold with rows of open-flame brass dish lamps on posts, where the other hold panels use hanging glass ship lanterns. If the next generation also fails, v07 is the least-bad fallback (tails: Keshavrao about 0.748,0.328; Nagoji about 0.371,0.245).
decisions.correction: Keep the closed, flooded, storm-dark ship's hold from 5.4 and v07. Low timber deck beams close off the whole top of the frame: no sky, no fog, no daylight. Light comes only from two or three hanging glass ship lanterns, with no brass dish lamps on posts. Water is knee to thigh deep. There are ABSOLUTELY NO guards, soldiers, sailors, morions, halberds, pikes, armour or gallery anywhere in the hold; the only people present are chained prisoners in rags. Composition along one waist-high pen beam, seen side-on and wide. In the LEFT half, Nagoji (left) and Keshavrao (right of him), each in an empty iron collar with wrists manacled and ankles hobbled. Nagoji holds up the iron ring they have just torn out of splintered wood, and its freed chain slithers off the beam into the water with a splash. Keshavrao has one bare foot braced against the beam, still kicking at it. In the RIGHT half, the next section's ring is still bolted fast into sound, unsplintered timber. Two or three chained prisoners there have stopped pulling, hands slack on their chain, and have turned their heads to stare left after Nagoji and Keshavrao, faces clearly visible. Keep the upper left above Nagoji and Keshavrao low-detail dark beams for two balloons, and the water along the bottom plain for two captions.

decisions.issues:
Neither candidate is acceptable because both break the chapter 3 irons: wrist manacles joined by a short chain about a forearm long. The r2 five-lens review already confirmed this as a major fault in v05, and the v06 edit did not fix it.

What both get right: the lantern-lit closed hold with barrels, crates and rope-wrapped posts, which matches pages 2 and 3. Nagoji is on the left with the thick curled moustache, clean chin, gold stud, torn ochre sleeveless tunic, cream dhoti, bandaged hands and collar with side ring, and his left inner forearm is covered by bandage. Keshavrao is on the right with short ragged hair, a faint moustache, grey-brown rags and a collar. The bandaged grip on Keshavrao's forearm is legible, and there is no text, gore or noose.

v05: Keshavrao's arms are flung to full span, a cuff on each wrist with no chain between them. Nagoji's wrists are far more than a forearm apart, and a long looping chain runs from his lower cuff up through the grip and merges with the chain from his collar ring. It reads as one long collar-to-wrist chain, not a short chain between his wrists.

v06 (edit of v05): Keshavrao is unchanged, still at full span with unjoined cuffs. Nagoji's collar ring is now empty, which breaks 3.2's slack collar chain and 4.1's pen chain. His wrist chain is now two unconnected pieces: a short stub from the lower cuff vanishes behind the tunic hem, and a second length hangs from under the gripping cuff past Keshavrao's cuff to a free end in mid-air. So his wrists are still visibly unjoined.

Both frames also paint a thin black border inside the image.
decisions.correction: Keep the same lantern-lit closed hold (barrels, crates, rope-wrapped posts, wet tilted planking, no sky), the same costumes, faces and lighting, and the same left-right placement. Redraw the irons and poses as follows. Keshavrao, on the right, slides away down the tilting deck with BOTH manacled wrists close together, no more than a forearm apart. Both of his hands claw at the iron hoop of the barrel on the right, and his fingers are slipping off it. A short chain of about eight to ten links is visibly attached at both ends and hangs between his two cuffs. Nagoji, on the left, lunges toward him with BOTH hands forward and close together. His bandaged hand clamps round Keshavrao's forearm just above the cuff, and his other bandaged hand is right beside it. His own short chain, about a forearm long and visibly attached to both of his cuffs, swings and strikes Keshavrao's cuff at the grip. His left forearm stays wrapped in bandage from wrist to mid-forearm, with the inner side turned down, away from camera. Each man's collar ring carries its own separate slack chain that runs off to the side and up out of frame, toward the pen chain. The collar chains never join or touch the wrist chains. Every chain in the image is attached at both ends or runs out of the frame; no chain ends loose in mid-air. Do not paint a border or frame line inside the image.

decisions.issues: Neither candidate is acceptable. v11 stages the beat well. The musket is large across the foreground and has come to rest against a thick beam with an iron ring near the foot of the ladder. It lies a clear few yards from the pens, and Nagoji, Keshavrao and the background prisoners have all turned toward it. But it breaks the chapter 3 bible row. Neither Nagoji nor Keshavrao (nor any prisoner) wears the hinged iron collar, and there is no collar-to-collar pen chain; the chains hang from the pen posts to the floor instead. No short chain joins the wrist manacles, and only single cuffs show. The pair are also swapped, with Keshavrao on the left and Nagoji on the right, which reverses the Nagoji-left / Keshavrao-right rule and the order in 2.3. The musket butt is drawn as a round tube with a brass cap and a hole in it, not a shaped stock. v10 has the right irons and identities, but the five-lens r2 review flagged it as a major failure and that still holds. The two leads fill the panel. The musket is a small, cropped object in the bottom-right corner, with no ladder and no beam to stop against, and the background prisoners look at the camera, not the gun. The musket also lies about a foot from Keshavrao's feet, which contradicts 2.4, 'Too far to reach.'
decisions.correction: Keep this exact composition. Use a low camera at floor level on the wet planks. The flintlock musket lies large across the lower foreground, with its butt toward the camera at lower left, and has come to rest against a thick upright beam with an iron ring at the right. Behind the beam, the ladder rises toward the hatch at upper right. In the middle ground, across a clear stretch of empty wet floor that puts the gun obviously out of reach, are the plank pens: Nagoji and Keshavrao in the nearest pen and rows of prisoners behind, every head turned to stare at the musket. Lantern light, dark timbers. Fix these: NAGOJI IS ON THE LEFT and KESHAVRAO ON THE RIGHT, seated shoulder to shoulder. Every prisoner, including both of them, wears a rigid hinged iron collar with a ring at the side, and ONE pen chain runs collar to collar through those side rings, drooping in slack loops along the plank between the men. No chains hang from posts to the floor, and none are vertical. Each man's two wrist manacles are joined by a short slack chain about a forearm long, and his ankle cuffs by a short hobble chain. Nagoji keeps his bandaged hands and wrists, curled moustache, clean chin and small gold stud, with his left forearm under the ragged ochre tunic flap. Draw the musket as a proper 18th-century flintlock: a shaped wooden butt with a flat brass butt plate, not a round tube. Keep the top eighth of the frame as plain dark ceiling beams with no lanterns in it, for the two captions.

decisions.issues: Neither candidate is acceptable. v08 gets the close two-shot right. Nagoji is on the left, looking up, with a clean chin, curled moustache, gold stud and bandaged wrists, his left forearm covered by bandage. Keshavrao is on the right, glancing down-right. Both wear collars joined by one pen chain. But it has three setting and story errors. (1) The hatch grating at top left shows bright blue sky and white clouds in the middle of the storm. (2) The seawater is a choppy pool up to their laps and wrists, not a thin thread across the boards past their feet. That contradicts 'starting to thread', 2.4's thin current, and 3.1, where the first wave brings water to the knee. (3) At the right edge, a musket stands almost upright and very close, in front of a standing figure (a garment hem and a dark leg). It reads as someone holding a gun beside them in the hold and puts the musket within Keshavrao's reach, against 2.1 and 2.4. v07 is the old pick, which the five-lens r2 review flagged as major. It is a wide full-figure shot, not 'Close'. The two men sit about a metre apart in an open aisle among barrels, with no pen boards and no other prisoners, which breaks from 2.1. Keshavrao looks down at the floor, not at the musket.
decisions.correction: Keep v08's close two-shot and identities exactly. Use a tight low camera on the two men seated shoulder to shoulder with their knees drawn up, framed from the tops of their heads down to their bare feet. Nagoji is on the left, face tilted up toward the hatch; Keshavrao is on the right, eyes turned down-right toward the musket, which stays OUT OF FRAME. Both wear iron collars with side rings joined by the one slack pen chain, wrist manacles, and ankle cuffs with a short hobble chain. Nagoji keeps his bandaged hands and wrists and his left forearm covered; Keshavrao's hands are thin and bare. Fix these: the floor is wet planking with only a thin trickle of seawater threading across the boards around their bare feet and hobble chains, NO standing or choppy water, no water above the ankles. The right edge of the frame shows only the pen's upright boards: no musket, no guard, no standing figure, legs or garment anywhere in frame. The background is the upright plank boards of the same lantern-lit pen as the previous panel, with one or two dim chained prisoners behind. There is no visible sky; if the hatch shows at all, it is a small square of flat grey storm light with rain, never blue sky or clouds. Leave the upper right corner above Keshavrao's head as plain dark boards for his line, which is read first, and a plain dark area between their heads, a little lower, for Nagoji's reply.
